description: Treat constructible graphs as a graph-grammar search space rather than as flat combinatorial objects. Learn or hand-design a small production system whose derivation trees already respect the user's recursive construction law, then search over that grammar with exact score extraction at each node.
mathematical_formalization: Let \Gamma be a grammar whose productions rewrite typed interface graphs into larger typed interface graphs. Each derivation tree D\in\mathcal{L}(\Gamma) maps to a legal constructible graph G(D). Search \Gamma for D minimizing S(G(D),R(D),T(D)) subject to exact extractability of R(D),T(D).
analogical_connections: The constructible graph definition is already a restricted graph grammar waiting to be exploited.
Parser-controlled induction becomes a way to discover reusable certificate macrocells.
RoboGrammar-style heuristic search suggests how to rank partial derivations without expanding every branch.
implementation_hypothesis: Seed the grammar with tiny exact certificates and interface summaries. Use best-first or beam search on partial derivations, ranking them by extracted score lower bounds and interface compatibility, while keeping every candidate verifier-compatible by construction.
experiment_seed: Start with a grammar over 3-6 interface types and 2-level derivations only. Compare grammar search against raw edge-by-edge local-rule search on the same budget and accept the grammar approach only if it finds better exact scores or better transfer across scales.

closest_prior_art.title: RoboGrammar: Graph Grammar for Terrain-Optimized Robot Design
Pattern Problems related to the Arithmetic Kakeya Conjecture

novelty_claim: The novelty is a parser-controlled search over exact arithmetic Kakeya certificate grammars, not graph grammar induction in general.
differentiation: Unlike generic graph-grammar work, every derivation must decode to a legal witness in the user's certificate format. That verifier coupling is the part that makes the bridge nontrivial.
